subject: Architecture
title: The Sagrada Família: 140 Years and Counting
description: A 60-second lesson on The Sagrada Família: 140 Years and Counting.

hook.text: Construction of the Sagrada Família began in 1882. It still isn't finished.

buildup.text: Antoni Gaudí designed it as a 'Bible in stone' with 18 towers representing apostles and Christ.

discovery.text: Gaudí used hanging chain models upside down to calculate the natural curves of his arches.

twist.text: Gaudí was killed by a tram in 1926. He was so shabbily dressed that nobody recognized him.

climax.text: 3D printing and computer modeling are now finishing what Gaudí could only sketch by hand.

punchline.text: He knew he'd never see it finished. He built it anyway.

quiz.question: How did Gaudí calculate the natural curves for his arches?
options: He used early computers imported from England
He hung chain models upside down
He copied curves from seashells and plants

details.summary: Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and remains unfinished over 140 years later. Its organic forms, inspired by trees and natural geometry.
details.whyItMatters: The Sagrada Família demonstrates that great architecture can transcend its creator's lifetime. Gaudí designed a building so complex that completing it required technology he could never have imagined.
takeaways: Under construction since 1882, still unfinished after 140+ years
Organic forms use catenary arches and hyperboloid surfaces
Computer-aided design was needed to realize Gaudí's vision

faq.question: When will the Sagrada Família be finished?
faq.answer: Completion was targeted for 2026 (the centenary of Gaudí's death), but COVID-19 delays pushed the date further. The main tower of Jesus Christ was topped in 2023. Much interior work remains. The building has been consecrated and holds services while construction continues around worshippers.

faq.question: How did Gaudí design without computers?
faq.answer: Gaudí used hanging chain models — weighted strings that formed natural catenary curves. He photographed these models upside down to visualize the arch forms. He also built plaster and wire scale models.
